Here’s why agent swarms are going to be a very big deal. We can finally make compute a critical variable in a large number of important tasks in the economy which wasn’t possible before.

There’s a large amount of work in the world that is essentially only constrained by the amount of time that we put into research, data processing, discovery work, running tests, and more. All of this work is bottlenecked by our ability to plan, execute, review, and coordinate everything happening in these workflows. Which means we basically do very little of them today relative to their economic value. 

Agent swarms are the first real ability to parallelize this work in a way where - in theory - the only parameter that matters is how much compute you throw at the problem. Cyber security, life sciences or material science research, trading, QA testing, data processing, and many other fields are essentially compute constrained problems in the limit once models are good enough at these tasks.

The breakthrough is that in a world where agents can use tools, write code, process data, have strong domain depth, and can coordinate with each other, you can begin to solve arbitrarily complex problems by setting the right goals and applying enough tokens to the problem. This changes a lot of fields as well as even the competitive dynamics in these fields.

The big bitter lesson question in the applied AI layer is that as models get better and better, what is the best way to diffuse that intelligence into an enterprise. 

Ironically, I’d argue that as models are getting more capable, and can handle longer running tasks and better tool use, the ability to differentiate on a domain by domain basis goes up instead of down. 

When models were quite limited in what they could do, ironically all you could be literally was a “wrapper” because you were effectively delivering tokens back to the user with a custom prompt or some limited RAG. 

But in a world of agents using tools, tasks that run on for hours or days, workflows that kick off agents, agent swarms that need to be coordinated against a goal, data sources that are domain specific, model routing that requires domain-specific routing, implementation that requires real change management of the workflow instead of “just type into this chat box”, it’s very very possible that specialization of these systems goes up more. 

Obviously this doesn’t apply to everything - the closer you are to the labs core use-cases the tougher this play gets, but I’d argue we’re going to see autonomous systems for a wide range of job functions that weren’t practical to build out before. We’ll see this in security, life sciences, healthcare, finance, manufacturing, and many other fields. Either way going to be a fun and wild couple of years.

We found DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 beats GPT 6 Sol on our multi-step offensive cybersecurity task. Sol was tested via the Daybreak trusted access program.

We have been building a cybersecurity benchmark based on simulated corporate networks. This is a valuable indicator for the cyber-risk a model poses if in the hands of a bad actor. We plan to make the full evaluation public in the coming weeks but wanted to share our first immediate finding here.

Today we’re releasing ClaimBench, our new benchmark targeted towards decision models. It tests whether a model can tell if a financial document supports, contradicts, or doesn’t address a claim.

We evaluated 15 models on 1,960 claims paired with 10-K excerpts, with Decider V1.2 leading the pack of decision models.

How do model routers compare to individual models on real agentic tasks? Introducing the Vals Router Index.

Routers promise to balance quality and cost across a fast-moving model frontier. We put that promise to the test with an independent evaluation of five routers (OpenRouter Auto, FireRouter, Ramp Router, Jev, Fugu Max) against every single model on the Vals Index, using the same agents, ~1,250 tasks and graders across finance, coding, law and tax.

We found that routing didn’t consistently deliver better value. Every router was beaten on both score and cost by at least one single model.
Reflection's Beam 1.0 now ranks #10 among all open-weight models, is the fastest model on the Vals Index, and is free to the public. https://t.co/WIDbWAfd16

Mistral has released new Speech models! Voxtral Small Transcribe 3 takes the #3 spot on the Artificial Analysis Speech to Text leaderboard, and Voxtral 3 TTS enters the top 12 in both Text to Speech arenas

@MistralAI has released Voxtral 3: a new Text to Speech model and three Speech to Text models (Small Transcribe 3, Mini Transcribe 3 and Mini Transcribe Realtime 3). We evaluated all of them.

Key takeaways:

➤ Speech to Text: Voxtral Small Transcribe 3 takes the #3 spot on the Artificial Analysis Speech to Text leaderboard with a 2.1% AA-WER Index, ahead of ElevenLabs Scribe v2 (2.2%) and Grok Voice Transcribe 2.0 (2.3%). Voxtral Mini Transcribe 3 lands at #5 with 2.2%.

➤ Streaming Speech to Text: Voxtral Mini Transcribe Realtime 3 scores 3.3% final-transcript AA-WER at the 960 ms setting (#6 of 46) and 3.6% at 480 ms, down from 5.2% for the previous Voxtral Mini Transcribe Realtime.

➤ Text to Speech, Provider Voice: Voxtral 3 TTS scores an Elo of 1,218 across 1,599 arena appearances, ranking #12 of 98, just behind Breeze TTS 2 at 1,221 and ahead of Inworld Realtime TTS-2 Flash and StepAudio 2.5 TTS at 1,216. It ranks #13 in English (US) and #12 in English (UK).

➤ Text to Speech, Controlled Voice: Voxtral 3 TTS scores 1,068 across 1,614 appearances, ranking #12 of 43 with the same 8 cloned voices, behind Eleven v3 at 1,072 and level with Ant Group's Ming-3.0-tts at 1,068. It ranks #10 in Assistants and #10 in English (UK).

➤ Pronunciation Robustness: Voxtral 3 TTS scores 84.4%, ranking #13 of 32 models, behind Qwen-Audio-3.1-TTS-Plus at 84.6% and ahead of HeyGen Voice at 83.2%. It ranks #3 in Standalone Terms at 93.9%.

➤ Pricing: Voxtral 3 TTS is priced at $13/1M characters, compared to Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS at $16.5/1M characters, Eleven v4 Turbo at $40/1M characters and Simba 3.2 at $6.6/1M characters.

Once Intelligence Index thresholds are reached, the cost of accessing that level of intelligence reduces fast. Reaching 30 on the Intelligence Index now costs 86x less per task than when first reached

Existing intelligence thresholds have become cheaper to reach, while the highest-scoring model costs more than the highest-scoring from one year ago.

Key takeaways:

➤ Reaching 20 is 123x cheaper than ~13 months ago; reaching 40 is 33x cheaper than ~5 months ago: measured models first reached these thresholds in September 2025 and May 2026.

➤ GPT-6 Luna (high) reaches 30 for $0.03/task: @OpenAI's model is 86x cheaper per task than @AnthropicAI's Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Adaptive Reasoning, Max Effort), which first reached 30 in February 2026 at $2.49/task.

➤ Claude Haiku 5.5 (xhigh) is now cheapest to reach 40: it scores 41 at $0.12/task, 5% below GPT-6.1 Sol (low).

➤ Reaching 50 is 18x cheaper than when first reached: GPT-6.1 Sol (high) reaches it for $0.32/task.

➤ The highest measured score has risen from 21 to 58 in a year, at ~11x the cost: Claude Opus 5.5 (Adaptive Reasoning, Max Effort, Default Fallback) costs $5.98/task.

As of October 20, 2026, using measured v4.3.2 results and current prices, including for historical models.

part 4 of "software is taking off"

through recent discussions i realized many people saying "software is dead" were actually thinking about software engineering as a profession

so.. is software engineering dead?

when i was a kid, my mom was an accountant. when i was doing my homework in the evenings, I would hear the sound of her using abacus. it was very loud and noisy

over the years, the sound of pushing abacus became punching calculators, then typing on keyboards, and eventually making phone calls. she just retired a few years ago, as a director of an accounting team

if you thought of the accounting profession as "pushing abacus", it died a long time ago. but if you understood accountants' jobs are actually "helping businesses make the right financial decisions", you'll realize it'll never stop being relevant

so whether software engineering is dead pretty much all depends on your mindset on what the profession even is

if your definition is "i write code others tell me to write", yup that's already dead

if it's some form of "i write very good code", it's not quite dead yet, but i speculate it'll be dead within the next 1-3 years. i'll link in the thread below another post where i explained why

so what's the type of engineer that's seeing growing demand?

fig. 1 shows SWE overall seeing a growth in job posting in the US. it tells quite a story when that's happening during a year when coding agents have seen the craziest advancements and adoption

fig. 2 shows a lot of the growth came from senior, or AI related roles. i will touch on why below

fig. 3 shows the rise of FDEs

the growing demand for software engineers is for those who has the right capability to solve problems with high precision, agency, and leverage - these traits have always been desired long before AI came along, and are seeing no sign of stopping

just think - when two competing companies both have access to the same AI, who wins? it's going to be their humans that make the difference, and they are going to get as many of such humans as they can

the software engineering profession has never been about writing punch cards, writing assembly, or writing C. it's never been about using vim, emacs, or visual studio. the code, the tools, and the activities have always been changing nonstop

the profession has always been about "solving problems with software". now there are a lot more problems that just became solvable, and everyone has gained quite an insane amount of leverage - there's never been a better time
